#### When should I seek immediate medical attention for an STI?

You should seek immediate medical attention if: 

- Severe Symptoms
- Open Sores or Lesions
- Unusual Discharge
- Worsening Symptoms
- Known Exposure to HIV
- Allergic Reactions to treatment
- Mental Health Crisis

#### What should I do if the condom breaks during sex?

If you feel the condom break at any point before or during sex:

**1. Stop immediately!**

**2. Withdraw.**

**3. Carefully remove the broken condom and put on a new one.**

**4. Get tested.**
- It is a good idea for you and your partner to get tested for STDs a few weeks after the condom broke or before having sex with another partner.

> When a condom breaks, you can come into contact with sexual fluids that can spread STIs. STIs often do not show symptoms. So testing is the only way to know for sure whether you have one.

#### What are the signs and symptoms of an STI?

Most STIs do not have symptoms; they can be non-specific when symptoms occur. 

- General symptoms of an STI can include: 
- Unusual discharge
- Pain when peeing
- Lumps or skin growth around the genitals
- A rash
- Unusual vaginal bleeding
- Itchy
- Blisters, warts, or sores 

If you think you have contracted an STI, discuss it with your healthcare provider and get tested. 

Specific STI tests take several weeks or more to return results. In that time, abstain from sex. 

#### Suspect you have an STI?
If you think you have contracted an STI, discuss it with your healthcare provider and get tested.
[Find a clinic near you that has STI testing available.](https://www.google.com/maps/search/sti+clinic+near+me/@37.3529694,-122.0304432,13z/data=!3m1!4b1?hl=en&authuser=0)

#### How do I seek medical advice about a possible STI exposure?

1. Schedule an Appointment: Call a provider to schedule an evaluation appointment.
2. Explain Your Concerns: State that you think you may have an STI and provide details.
3. List Symptoms or Concerns: Mention any symptoms or concerns you have.
4. Clarify Follow-Up Steps: Understand your follow-up appointments or actions are necessary based on test results and treatment.
5. Seek Clarification: If you have questions, do not hesitate to ask.

Remember, seeking medical advice is important for diagnosis and timely treatment if necessary. Your provider is there to support you and provide care.

> **What To Ask Your Doctor:**
> - Ask About Testing: Ask about the types of tests that may be appropriate.
> - Ask About Treatment: If you have an STI, ask about available treatment and follow your prescription.

#### Why do I need to tell my partner about my STI?

If you have an active STI, it is normal to be nervous, worried, embarrassed, and even scared about telling a new or current sexual partner. 

The important thing is that you are truthful with them and do not delay in telling them. 

#### You Need To Tell Them to Protect Them.

**Your partner needs to know what is going on because their health is at risk:**
- STIs can cause serious health problems, especially if they are not found and treated.
- Telling a past or current partner gives that person a chance to get checked out and treated if needed.
- Telling a future partner lets that person make an informed decision about their own health.
- If you are treated for an STI but your partner is not, you can get re-infected.
- Not telling a partner about an STI after a confirmed diagnosis may be a criminal offense in some states.
- Some STIs can lower the chances of having babies in the future if not treated early on.

#### How do I tell my partner I have an STI?

### How to Tell Your Partner
**1. Prepare yourself to have this conversation.** 
- Learn about your diagnosis. When you are well-versed and know what you are dealing with, explaining everything to a partner or family is easier. 
- Mentally prepare. There could be many strong emotions and judgments. They may have to walk away.
> **Caring conversation tip:** It may help to say "I do not expect you to like anything I say today. That is OK. I know this is a lot to digest. But I respect you enough to tell you what is going on." 
##### Source: [Dr. Oluwatosin Goje, MD, Cleveland Clinic](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/h-how-to-tell-your-partner-you-have-an-std/)

**2. Be Upfront, Honest, and Caring.**

 Imagine the roles were reversed. What would you expect your partner to do and say if they were in your shoes? 
- Be direct and tell them before you have sex.
- Listen to your partner and encourage questions.
- Do not push them to make a decision then.

**3. Be proud of your intentions.** 
- Your willingness to have this hard conversation shows that you care about the other person and your relationship. We are more likely to trust and respect people who are honest (and brave!) enough to talk about tough topics like STIs.
> Blaming yourself is never the answer. Keep in mind that while you might think your recent diagnosis is a newer issue, there is always the possibility that you may have been exposed to herpes at a younger age or your STI was dormant for many years and is just now showing symptoms. In any case, having an STD is not shameful, and holding it against yourself will not help.

**Resources to help you have this difficult conversation**
- [Telling Your Partner You Have an STD](https://kidshealth.org/en/teens/stds-talk.html)
- [How To Tell Someone That You Have an STD or STI](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/h-how-to-tell-your-partner-you-have-an-std/)

#### How do I support someone who just found out they have an STI?

#### Receiving an STI diagnosis can be an emotional experience.

People commonly feel shock, fear, anger, guilt, and shame after receiving an STI diagnosis.

It is important to remember that these reactions are normal and that there is no reason to feel ashamed or guilty. 

Coping with an STI diagnosis can be challenging, but seeking emotional support from loved ones and healthcare providers can make a significant difference.

#### What should I say to someone who has shared their STI diagnosis with me?

If someone has trusted you enough to disclose their STI diagnosis to you, you can be kind and show care with your response: 
- "I am here for you, and I am glad you shared this with me."
- "Having an STI does not define who you are as a person."
- "You are not alone in this. Many people go through similar experiences."
- "It is important to remember that STIs are common, and they can happen to anyone."
- "Accidents happen. We all make mistakes. This does not make you a bad person."
- "Treatment is available, and you can take steps to manage this."
- "Your health is a top priority, and I am here to support you in any way I can."
- "Let us talk about how you can protect yourself and others in the future."
- "I care about you, and this does not change how I feel about you."

#### What should I NOT say to someone who has just disclosed their STI diagnosis?

- "This is your fault."
- "You should have been more careful."
- "I cannot believe you let this to happen."
- "You must have been promiscuous."
- "You brought this upon yourself."
- "I told you so."
- "You are disgusting"
- "You are dirty/unclean"
- "I can not be around you anymore."
- "You will never find someone who will accept you now."

#### Why is contraception important for preventing STIs?

Contraception can help prevent the spreading of an STI from one person to another.

Anybody who has oral, anal, or vaginal sex, or genital skin-to-skin contact with another person can get STIs. Almost all sexually active people get one at some point in their life.

#### How effective are condoms at preventing STIs?

Condoms are "barrier" method contraception tools and the only type of contraception that reduces your risk of both pregnancy and STIs, including HIV. 

Condoms must be used correctly and must be used every time you have sex to work.

#### Condoms Are Not Perfect Protection
Condoms cannot completely protect you and your partner from some STDs, like herpes, syphilis, or human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus that causes genital wart and cervical cancer. Condoms can break, slip, or leak, especially if they are not put on and taken off properly. 

 
- [external condoms](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/contraception/male-condoms/#:~:text=At%20a%20glance%3A%20condoms,clinics%20and%20some%20GP%20surgeries.) 98% effective protection

- [internal condoms](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/contraception/female-condoms/)- 95% effective protection

#### Which STIs have vaccines available?

Safe and Effective Vaccines are available for three viral STIs:

1. Hepatitis B
2. Hepatitis A 
3. Human Papillomavirus (HPV)

#### Who should get the Hepatitis B vaccine?

**[Hepatitis B Frequently Asked Questions | CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/hepatitis/hbv/bfaq.htm)**

**Hepatitis B vaccine is recommended for:**
- Sex partners of anyone who has hepatitis B
- Anyone who is sexually active but not in a long-term, monogamous relationship
- Those treated for STD/STIs
- Men who have sex with men

Others recommended for the hepatitis B vaccine include:
- All infants and children under age 19 who have not had the vaccine
- Injecting drug users who share needles
- Those living in households with someone who has hepatitis B
- Anyone whose work places them in contact with blood
- Those with HIV or chronic liver disease
- Individuals in correctional facilities
- Travelers to areas with a high prevalence of hepatitis B

#### Who should get the Hepatitis A vaccine?

**[Hepatitis A Frequently Asked Questions | CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/hepatitis/hav/afaq.htm#transmission)**

**Hepatitis A vaccine is recommended for all children and adolescents and people at higher risk:**
- International travelers
- Men who have sex with men
- People who use or inject drugs
- People with occupational risk for exposure
- People who anticipate close personal contact with an international adoptee
- People experiencing homelessness
- Anyone traveling to an area with a high prevalence of hepatitis A
- Those with hepatitis B or C

#### Who should get the HPV vaccine?

**[HPV Vaccination: What everyone Should Know | CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/vpd/hpv/public/)**

**The HPV vaccine is recommended at the age of 11 or 12 years but it can be for those under the age of 26.**

- The HPV vaccine does not treat existing HPV but can prevent new HPV infections. 
- It is not recommended for use during pregnancy.

#### How are bacterial STIs treated?

Certain STI tests take several weeks or more to return results. In that time, abstain from sex. 
NOTIFY your partners so they can get tested and treated

#### STIs Caused by Bacteria: Curable

- Antibiotics can cure many infections including gonorrhea, syphilis, chlamydia and trichomoniasis. Once you start antibiotic treatment, it is important to finish the entire prescription. 

- Stay away from sex for seven days until you have completed the antibiotic treatment.

- Women should retest in about three months because there is a high chance of reinfection. 
- If you have a curable it is important to complete a prescribed treatment. This is true even if you feel better before it is finished. 

- Do not have sexual contact until you finish your medicine.

#### How are viral STIs managed?

#### Viral STIs: Incuable but Manageable 
- There are plenty of treatments for Hepatitis B, herpes simplex virus (HSV), HIV, and human papillomavirus (HPV) that can help you live a healthy life, ease symptoms, and avoid passing the infection to other partners. 

- Most only cause mild symptoms or no symptoms at all but it is important to discuss options with your healthcare provider to develop a treatment plan. 

- Antiviral drugs can keep certain infections such as HIV or herpes suppressed but it is still possible to transmit to your partner. 
- Antivirals can keep infections in check for many years however, you will still carry the virus and can still transmit it, though the risk is lower. 
- The sooner you start treatment, the more effective it is.

#### How do I live with an STI long-term?

You are **NOT** less of a person because you have/had an STI.

Communication with future partners about your status 
If you have multiple sexual partners, you must share this information with each of them. 

- Be honest and open to questions from your partner(s) 

- Do your research about the STI

- Pick the right place to disclose your status where you are safest and most comfortable.

#### What questions should I ask my doctor about my STI?

Questions to ask your doctor:

- What STI have I contracted, and what are the symptoms and side effects? 
- What medication will I be on (if any), and how can my partner receive treatment? 
- Do I need to abstain from sex? For how long? 
- Should I test more often because of my status?
